item.title: Arrays
item.description:
Arrays#

So far, we have learned how to describe a thing using an object.

const student = {
 name: "Anu",
 age: 20,
 city: "Chennai"
};

This works very well when we have one thing.

But what happens when we have many things?

Suppose we have three students:

const student1 = {
 name: "Anu",
 age: 20
};

const student2 = {
 name: "Rahul",
 age: 19
};

const student3 = {
 name: "Meera",
 age: 20
};

What if we have thirty students?

What if we have three hundred?

We could keep giving every student a different variable name. But something feels wrong about that.

item.title: Loops
item.description:
Loops#

We have been asking the computer to do more and more interesting things.

We can give names to values. We can make decisions with if. We can organize data with objects. We can even draw things on the screen.

But there is one thing we haven’t really asked the computer to do yet:

Do something again.

You have already seen a loop, though.

Think back to the Raylib program we wrote.

item.title: JS Math Reference
item.description:
// ============================================================================
// JavaScript Math Reference
// ============================================================================
//
// A compact reference for common mathematical operations in JavaScript.
//
// ============================================================================



// ============================================================================
// ABSOLUTE VALUE
// ============================================================================

Math.abs(5); // 5
Math.abs(-5); // 5
Math.abs(0); // 0

Math.abs(10 - 15); // 5



// ============================================================================
// MINIMUM AND MAXIMUM
// ============================================================================

Math.min(2, 5); // 2
Math.min(10, 3, 7); // 3

Math.max(2, 5); // 5
Math.max(10, 3, 7); // 10

Math.min(-5, -2); // -5
Math.max(-5, -2); // -2



// ============================================================================
// SQUARE ROOT
// ============================================================================

Math.sqrt(9); // 3
Math.sqrt(16); // 4
Math.sqrt(2); // approximately 1.414

// The Pythagorean theorem:
//
// c = √(a² + b²)

Math.sqrt(3 ** 2 + 4 ** 2); // 5



// ============================================================================
// POWERS
// ============================================================================

Math.pow(2, 3); // 8
Math.pow(5, 2); // 25

// The ** operator does the same thing.

2 ** 3; // 8
5 ** 2; // 25



// ============================================================================
// ROUNDING
// ============================================================================

Math.floor(3.9); // 3
Math.floor(3.1); // 3
Math.floor(-3.1); // -4

Math.ceil(3.1); // 4
Math.ceil(3.9); // 4
Math.ceil(-3.1); // -3

Math.round(3.1); // 3
Math.round(3.5); // 4
Math.round(3.9); // 4

Math.trunc(3.9); // 3
Math.trunc(-3.9); // -3



// ============================================================================
// RANDOM NUMBERS
// ============================================================================

Math.random(); // A random number from 0 up to, but not including, 1.

Math.random(); // 0.374...
Math.random(); // 0.821...
Math.random(); // 0.092...



// ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Random integer
// ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

// A random integer from 0 through 9:

Math.floor(Math.random() * 10);

// A random integer from 0 through 99:

Math.floor(Math.random() * 100);

// A random integer from 1 through 10:

Math.floor(Math.random() * 10) + 1;



// ============================================================================
// CONSTANTS
// ============================================================================

Math.PI; // approximately 3.14159
Math.E; // approximately 2.71828

Math.SQRT2; // approximately 1.41421
Math.SQRT1_2; // approximately 0.70711



// ============================================================================
// TRIGONOMETRY
// ============================================================================
//
// JavaScript uses radians, not degrees.
//
// 180° = π radians
// 90° = π / 2 radians
//
// ============================================================================

Math.sin(0); // 0
Math.cos(0); // 1
Math.tan(0); // 0

Math.sin(Math.PI / 2); // 1
Math.cos(Math.PI); // -1



// ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Converting degrees to radians
// ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

const degrees = 90;
const radians = degrees * Math.PI / 180;

Math.sin(radians); // 1



// ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Converting radians to degrees
// ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

const radians = Math.PI;
const degrees = radians * 180 / Math.PI;

degrees; // 180



// ============================================================================
// INVERSE TRIGONOMETRY
// ============================================================================

Math.asin(1); // approximately π / 2
Math.acos(1); // 0
Math.atan(1); // approximately π / 4

Math.atan2(1, 1); // approximately π / 4



// ============================================================================
// LOGARITHMS AND EXPONENTS
// ============================================================================

Math.exp(1); // e

Math.log(Math.E); // 1
Math.log(1); // 0

Math.log10(100); // 2
Math.log2(8); // 3



// ============================================================================
// SIGN
// ============================================================================

Math.sign(10); // 1
Math.sign(-10); // -1
Math.sign(0); // 0



// ============================================================================
// USEFUL COMBINATIONS
// ============================================================================

// Distance between two points on a number line:

Math.abs(a - b);


// Distance between two points (x1, y1) and (x2, y2):

Math.sqrt(
 (x2 - x1) ** 2 +
 (y2 - y1) ** 2
);


// Clamp a value between a minimum and maximum:

Math.min(Math.max(value, minimum), maximum);


// Round a number to the nearest integer:

Math.round(value);


// Round down:

Math.floor(value);


// Round up:

Math.ceil(value);

item.title: Objects in Raylib
item.description:
Objects in Raylib#

We have learned about objects in JavaScript.

So far, we have mostly looked at objects as a way of putting related information together:

const student = {
 name: "Ravi",
 age: 20,
};

The useful thing about this is not the curly braces. The useful thing is that we can give a shape to something we are thinking about.

Raylib has many things that naturally have more than one piece of information.

A colour has several components.

item.title: Objects part 2
item.description:
Visualise it#

At this point, it can be useful to stop reading and experiment with a visualiser.

Try entering small examples such as:

const a = {
 x: 10,
};

const b = a;

b.x = 20;

Watch what happens when a and b refer to the same object.

Then try:

let a = {
 x: 10,
};

let b = a;

b = {
 x: 20,
};

Pay attention to the difference.

The visualiser is not a substitute for understanding the code.

Use it to test your mental model.

item.title: Objects
item.description:
Objects#

You have now written enough JavaScript to run into an interesting problem.

You have variables.

You have functions.

You have started writing programs that are a little larger than a few lines.

And now you may have noticed something.

Sometimes, several values belong together.

Suppose we want to describe a person.

We might write:

const name = "Asha";
const age = 20;
const city = "Mysuru";

There is nothing wrong with this.

But look at those three variables.

They all describe the same thing.

item.title: Particle Detector 2
item.description:
Extension — Scan in Two Directions#

Our particle detector has so far been scanning from left to right and back again.

That means we have been thinking about ranges along the horizontal direction.

But our region of space has two dimensions.

Why should we only scan horizontally?

A particle detector could also scan from top to bottom.

A New Direction#

Add another scanner to your simulation.

This scanner should move vertically.

item.title: Simple JS Practice
item.description:
JavaScript Practice#

Solve the following problems in JavaScript.

You have not learned traditional loops yet, so do not use for, while, or similar loops. Use recursion whenever you need to repeat an operation.

Write a separate function for each problem.

1. Simple Interest#

Write a function that calculates simple interest.

The function should take:

  • principal amount
  • rate of interest
  • time

and return the simple interest.

For example:

simpleInterest(1000, 5, 2) → 100

2. Compound Interest#

Write a function that calculates compound interest.

item.title: Particle Detector
item.description:
Scanning for Particles#

Imagine that we have sent a particle detector into space.

The detector is looking at a small region of space around it. It moves from one side of the region to the other, scanning for particles as it goes.

Our job is to build a simulation of this detector.

You will build the simulation in several steps. Each step adds one small idea to the previous one.

item.title: More about functions
item.description:
Function calls inside function calls#

So far, you have seen function calls like this:

double(5);

When you see this, you know that double(5) is an expression. The function runs, and eventually the expression produces a value.

Let’s make the expression a little more interesting.

Suppose we have:

function double(number) {
 return number * 2;
}

function addOne(number) {
 return number + 1;
}

Now consider:

addOne(double(5));

Don’t run it yet.

What value should addOne receive?

Think about what has to happen first.

item.title: Functions
item.description:
You have now started writing JavaScript programs in files.

Until now, you have mostly been asking JavaScript questions in the REPL:

> 10 % 2 === 0
true

> 17 % 2 === 0
false

Now you can put those expressions into a program, save the program in a file, and run it.

Today, we are going to look at a problem that appears very quickly when you start writing larger programs:

item.title: Const, let, if etc
item.description:
From the REPL to the Editor#

So far, you have been programming in the REPL.

You have typed expressions such as:

5 + 3;

and:

10 > 5 && 20 < 30;

JavaScript evaluates them and the REPL shows you the result.

You have also spent time drawing expression trees.

You have learned to look at an expression, break it into smaller expressions, and follow the order in which those expressions are evaluated.

Now we are going to change something.

item.title: JS Reference
item.description:
// ============================================================================
// JavaScript Language Reference
// ============================================================================
//
// A compact reference of JavaScript syntax and expressions.
// Every example in this file is valid JavaScript.
//
// ============================================================================



// ============================================================================
// COMMENTS
// ============================================================================

// This is a line comment.

/*
This is a
block comment.
*/



// ============================================================================
// LITERALS
// ============================================================================


// ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Numbers
// ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

0; // Zero is a valid number.
5; // A number evaluates to itself.
5.0; // Integers and decimals are both numbers.
5.25; // Numbers can have a fractional part.
-100.9999; // Numbers can be negative.
1e6; // Scientific notation for large numbers.
1e-3; // Scientific notation for small numbers.
0xff; // Hexadecimal literal (255).
0b1010; // Binary literal (10).
0o755; // Octal literal (493).
Infinity; // Positive infinity.
-Infinity; // Negative infinity.
NaN; // Represents "Not a Number".


// ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Booleans
// ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

true; // Boolean true.
false; // Boolean false.


// ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Strings
// ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

""; // The empty string.
"Hello"; // Double-quoted string.
'Hello'; // Single-quoted string.
`Hello`; // Template string using backticks.
"Hello\nWorld"; // Escape sequences insert special characters.


// ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Other Primitive Values
// ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

undefined; // Represents the absence of a value.
null; // Represents an intentional empty value.



// ============================================================================
// VARIABLES
// ============================================================================

let score = 0; // Declare a mutable variable.
let lives = 3; // Variables can be declared independently.

score = 100; // Variables can be reassigned.
score = score + 1; // Variables can use their current value.
lives = lives - 1; // Updating a variable is a common operation.

const width = 800; // Declare an immutable variable.
const height = 600; // Constants cannot be reassigned.



// ============================================================================
// ARITHMETIC OPERATORS
// ============================================================================


// ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Binary Arithmetic
// ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

5 + 3; // Addition.
5 - 3; // Subtraction.
5 * 3; // Multiplication.
5 / 2; // Division can produce decimals.
5 % 2; // Remainder after division.
2 ** 8; // Exponentiation (2 raised to the power of 8).


// ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Unary Arithmetic
// ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

let x = 5;

+x; // Unary plus converts a value to a number.
-x; // Unary minus negates a number.

++x; // Increment before the expression is evaluated.
x++; // Increment after the expression is evaluated.

--x; // Decrement before the expression is evaluated.
x--; // Decrement after the expression is evaluated.


// ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Compound Assignment
// ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

let y = 10;

y += 5; // Equivalent to y = y + 5.
y -= 2; // Equivalent to y = y - 2.
y *= 3; // Equivalent to y = y * 3.
y /= 4; // Equivalent to y = y / 4.
y %= 2; // Equivalent to y = y % 2.
y **= 3; // Equivalent to y = y ** 3.


// ============================================================================
// COMPLEX ARITHMETIC EXPRESSIONS
// ============================================================================

2 + 3 * 5; // Multiplication happens before addition (17).

(2 + 3) * 5; // Parentheses change the order of evaluation (25).

10 - 2 * 3; // Multiplication happens before subtraction (4).

(10 - 2) * 3; // Parentheses force subtraction first (24).

20 / 2 + 5; // Division happens before addition (15).

20 / (2 + 3); // Parentheses change the divisor (4).

2 * 3 + 4 * 5; // Operators of the same precedence are evaluated left to right (26).

(2 * (3 + 4)) * 5; // Parentheses can be nested.

2 ** 3 * 4; // Exponentiation happens before multiplication (32).

2 * 3 ** 4; // Exponentiation has higher precedence than multiplication (162).

-(2 + 3); // Unary minus applies to the grouped expression (-5).

-2 ** 2; // Exponentiation happens before unary minus (-4).

(-2) ** 2; // Parentheses make the negative number the base (4).


// ============================================================================
// COMPARISON OPERATORS
// ============================================================================

5 == "5"; // Loose equality converts values before comparing.
5 != "6"; // Loose inequality also performs type coercion.

5 === 5; // Strict equality compares both type and value.
5 !== "5"; // Strict inequality compares both type and value.

5 < 10; // Less than.
5 > 2; // Greater than.
5 <= 5; // Less than or equal.
5 >= 5; // Greater than or equal.



// ============================================================================
// BOOLEAN OPERATORS
// ============================================================================

!true; // Logical NOT inverts a boolean.
true && false; // Logical AND requires both operands to be true.
true || false; // Logical OR requires at least one operand to be true.

5 > 3 && 10 < 20; // Boolean expressions can be combined with AND.
5 < 3 || 10 < 20; // OR succeeds if either expression is true.
!(5 === 5); // NOT negates the result of an expression.



// ============================================================================
// BITWISE OPERATORS
// ============================================================================

5 & 3; // Bitwise AND.
5 | 3; // Bitwise OR.
5 ^ 3; // Bitwise XOR.
~5; // Bitwise NOT.

5 << 1; // Shift bits left by one position.
5 >> 1; // Arithmetic right shift.
5 >>> 1; // Logical right shift.



// ============================================================================
// ASSIGNMENT OPERATORS
// ============================================================================

let value = 10;

value = 20; // Replace the current value.

value &&= 30; // Assign only if the current value is truthy.
value ||= 40; // Assign only if the current value is falsy.

let answer = null;

answer ??= 42; // Assign only if the value is null or undefined.



// ============================================================================
// TYPE OPERATOR
// ============================================================================

typeof 5; // Evaluates to "number".
typeof true; // Evaluates to "boolean".
typeof "Hello"; // Evaluates to "string".
typeof undefined; // Evaluates to "undefined".
typeof null; // Evaluates to "object" (historical JavaScript quirk).
typeof NaN; // NaN is still a number.



// ============================================================================
// TRUTHINESS
// ============================================================================

Boolean(true); // true remains true.
Boolean(false); // false remains false.

Boolean(1); // Non-zero numbers are truthy.
Boolean(0); // Zero is falsy.

Boolean("Hello"); // Non-empty strings are truthy.
Boolean(""); // The empty string is falsy.

Boolean(null); // null is falsy.
Boolean(undefined); // undefined is falsy.
Boolean(NaN); // NaN is falsy.



// ============================================================================
// CONDITIONAL EXPRESSIONS
// ============================================================================

true ? "yes" : "no"; // Chooses between two values.
5 > 3 ? 1 : 0; // The condition may be any boolean expression.



// ============================================================================
// STRING OPERATIONS
// ============================================================================

"Hello" + " World"; // Strings can be concatenated.
"Score: " + 10; // Non-strings are converted automatically.
`Score: ${10}`; // Template strings support interpolation.
"Hello\nWorld"; // Escape sequences create special characters.
"JavaScript".length; // Strings have useful properties.
